An old industrial site in Wheeling could become part of West Virginia’s next technology push.

As reported by WBOY, Silicon Foundation Energy LLC has purchased the former Centre Foundry & Machine Company property in Warwood, with plans to turn the Ohio River site into a phased data center and energy technology campus.

The property, located at 74 Warwood Avenue, was acquired for $1.5 million through a deed transfer tied to four parcels.

The project starts with a planned 10-megawatt modular data center system, paired with battery energy storage infrastructure. A second phase would expand the site to 20 to 30 megawatts.

If fully developed, the company says the campus could eventually reach 100 megawatts and operate as a regional compute hub.

The location carries deep industrial history. Centre Foundry’s roots in Wheeling go back to the 1800s, and the company moved to the Warwood site in 1923. For decades, it was tied to coal mining, iron castings, heavy molds and manufacturing work.

Now, the pitch is different: servers, GPUs, power systems and possibly battery manufacturing.

The proposal also arrives as West Virginia debates what data centers actually bring to local communities. Jobs, taxes, power demand and local control remain open questions.

For Wheeling, it’s another old mining and steel-era property being pulled into a new industrial argument.

While there is a push by some politicians of both parties to singularly blame, and in some cases scapegoat, datacenters for rising electricity prices, data from the U.S. Department of Energy’s U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) tells a much different story.

EIA’s most recent Electric Power Monthly on January 26 found that the nationwide average cost of residential electricity was 17.78 cents per kilowatt-hour (kWh) for the month of November 2025. That is up 5.5% from a year ago. It exceeds the Consumer Price Index (CPI) for that period, continuing a disturbing trend that began in 2021, long before the datacenter boom took off.

If datacenters are the singular reason for high electricity prices, then the states with the most of them should be in dire straits, pricewise. They are not.

A January 2026 study from the American Edge Project found that the two states with the most datacenters are, by far, Virginia (663) and Texas (405). These two states account for 26% of all U.S. datacenters.

Yet the average residential electricity rate in Virginia is 15.94 cents per kWh, more than 10% less than the national average. Yes, those costs have increased over the past year, and by slightly more than the national increase (8.2% vs. 5.5%), while Virginia has gained an influx of high-paying jobs, tax revenue, and other economic activity.

In Texas, the average residential electricity rate is 16.04 cents per kWh, 9.8% less than the national average. Over the past year, in energy-friendly Texas, residential electricity prices have risen 2.3%.

At the other end of the cost spectrum is Vermont, home of Senator Bernie Sanders, who has aggressively sought to demonize datacenters. Vermont has the fewest datacenters in the country – three. Yet Vermont’s residential electric rates are 36% above the national average, an onerous financial burden, especially in a state that does not receive the vast economic benefits of datacenters.

Electricity costs have risen faster than the CPI over the past five years due to systemic problems: a shortage of supply (power plants), an aging transmission grid prone to bottlenecks, and regulatory inertia, including intractable permitting delays.

Datacenters can be catalysts for breaking these chains in our electrical system and revitalizing it, so that it not only meets our needs but does so at a lower cost. There is ample precedent for this.

Since electricity was first invented and was initially available only to the wealthy, its costs have trended lower. Despite significant price increases since 2021, according to the Federal Reserve, average residential electricity prices fell by 14.6% from 1978 to 2026 when measured in real dollars, that is, adjusted for inflation.

It is time to accelerate electricity production so that the increased supply dwarfs the rising demand from datacenters, new manufacturing facilities, homes that want to use more electronic devices, and other factors.

With many Americans facing high electricity bills amid the current cold snap, constructive dialogue should begin immediately, using the EIA data and a sober assessment of the immense electricity challenges now facing the country.

A Texas Senate Finance Committee hearing held July 27 examined the state’s sales tax exemptions for data center projects, which could cost the state $3.3 billion in forgone taxes during the 2028-29 budget cycle.

In 2013, the Texas Legislature passed House Bill 1223, which exempted some data centers from paying sales tax on electricity costs, cooling systems, emergency generators and IT equipment. The legislature estimated this would cost about $14.6 million during the bill’s first two years.

In 2015, lawmakers expanded the incentive to larger data centers. Those projects qualify for the same state sales tax exemptions, but also receive them for a longer period and can qualify for local tax exemptions.

“This just shows you how fast the technology has changed, because we literally passed a bill in 2015 … that had a $15 million fiscal note. And now, with everything that’s changed, the exemptions are in the billions of dollars,” State Sen. Paul Bettencourt, R-Houston, said.

The fiscal burden grew rapidly since 2020, when just 10 data centers received tax breaks in Texas. As of July 2026, 138 data centers were certified for the exemption, with five more applications pending.

Several senators questioned whether the state knows how many additional projects are in development.

“There may be some that haven’t come yet … there’s a lot of deliberate secrecy involved in these developmental plans,” said Brad Reynolds, with the Texas Comptroller’s Revenue Estimating Division.

Texas’ incentives continue to attract some of the nation’s largest data center projects, which have been driven by demand for artificial intelligence and cloud computing. Lawmakers spent much of the hearing weighing whether the state’s incentives should continue unchanged or be revisited when the Legislature meets in 2027.

[Excerpt:]  AI companies want to capture the value created by entire industries. That concentration of wealth and power is society’s greatest risk

Thu 9 Jul 2026 11.00 EDT

Opposition to AI datacenters has emerged as a primary theme in US politics, one that – surprisingly – doesn’t fall along party lines. We applaud people coming together for constructive debate on any issue, and agree that communities need to evaluate whether any economic benefits these datacenters bring is worth their costs. Still, we worry that a focus on datacenters obscures the larger impacts of AI on people’s lives: the concentration of power of AI companies, and their widespread political and financial influence.

Local datacenter opposition is grounded in legitimate concerns about misallocation of land resources when housing is at a premium, pressures on already higher energy prices, and localized environmental impact. Unlike other resource-consuming and polluting industrial facilities, datacenters produce very few jobs. The fact that US opposition to datacenters seems to be most fierce among lower-income communities reflects righteous indignation with an inequitable bargain, where tech companies and developers profit from exploiting local resources but offer little in return. On a global scale, their carbon footprint could grow unsustainably if usage accelerates. And all this is in aid of a technology that many fear will propagate misinformation, take their jobs, or even cause existential risks for humanity.

For some, datacenter opposition may feel like the only tangible mechanism for registering their concern, disapproval, or even anger about AI. The problem is that this may be exactly what the AI companies are banking on. They can overcome the protest when it matters to them, and live with a significant fraction of proposals being defeated. More importantly, focusing political opponents on the datacenter issue obscures the bigger prize they’re after.

While there is a staggering three-quarters of $1tn being spent on datacenter infrastructure by US companies this year alone, this investment should be taken in perspective. The market for enterprise software, for example, is about twice this size. And it’s small compared with what these companies actually want.

AI companies have their eyes set on capturing all the value created by entire industries. The technology has arguably already conquered customer service and consumer sales. But on the horizon are bigger targets, such as enterprise software development, creative design, management and even legal services. In AI companies and their allies’ vision of the future, AI replaces teachers and doctors. The companies would rather spend time fighting resistance to how fast they are building computing infrastructure than dealing with issues of how their products should be used in those fields, or how those fields should be protected from their products.

And while datacenter opposition campaigns have been successful in building widespread appeal, their effectiveness in the US is mixed. They seem to be most successful when organizing against speculative, early-stage datacenter proposals that have a relatively low likelihood to ever see fruition. Meanwhile, advanced-stage, well-capitalized datacenter projects have proven to have the resources to overcome local opposition. An OpenAI- and Oracle-backed facility in Saline township, Michigan, is breaking ground on construction even after local officials voted to reject it. The developers sued the town of 3,000 and forced a settlement that involved their project going forward. Meanwhile, the Trump administration, a vigorous ally of corporate AI, has signalled its willingness to advance AI infrastructure development by overriding state objections and even using federal lands.

Also consider that rampant datacenter development may be a momentary spike rather than a longstanding concern. Demand for the centralized computing that datacenters provide may well decline over time. The leading Chinese labs, such as Z.ai, are innovating in technical mechanisms to make frontier-class models smaller and cheaper to run. AI power users have become adept at miniaturizing open weight models, ones published free for anyone to download and use, to run locally on their own computers. Apple and Google both support infrastructure stacks for running AI models directly on mobile phones. It could be that the current mania for datacenters will look like the fiber optic cable bubble from the early 2000s, as demand shifts to smaller models and AI usage on people’s own devices.

For those concerned primarily with affordability and environmental protection, singling out datacenter construction is misplaced. Energy rates and inflation today seem to be most visibly affected by the US-Iran war. The US is disinvesting in long-term energy security by ceding the renewable energy industry to China and actively cancelling climate commitments. Consider that 10% of global carbon emissions stem from heating buildings, which dwarfs energy use by AI and could be cut fivefold by using heat pumps powered by renewable energy. With respect to housing affordability, federal housing subsidies have changed little over three decades, in inflation-adjusted terms, even as housing costs have spiked and homeowners have enjoyed robust tax incentives.

As for AI itself, the concentration of power and wealth in these tech companies is the greatest existential risk facing society today. This means we must limit corporate power, especially corporations’ ability to exploit the public and manipulate our political system.

Opposing datacenters should be just a starting point. We can advocate for states to regulate AI, to reject irresponsible uses of the technology, and shape corporate behavior. We can fight for AI computation to be taxed, so that the public can capture some of the profit of AI use while also forcing AI companies to internalize more of the energy and environmental consequences associated with its use. And we all can join the global movement for Public AI, an alternative ecosystem for AI that is developed under public control with an incentive structure to create public benefit rather than private profit.

The US midterm elections present ample opportunity for those seeking to control the AI political agenda. In the recent New York congressional Democratic primary, Pacs linked to the dueling AI companies Anthropic and OpenAI spent millions of dollars lobbying for or against “AI safety”, the idea that we must urgently monitor and prevent people from using AI to cause catastrophic harms. We’re already seeing a similar dynamic play out in races in Massachusetts and other states.

Why would Anthropic and OpenAI – bitter industry rivals but fundamentally on the same side politically – support opposing viewpoints? Because they both ultimately profit from the mystique: the idea that their products are so powerful that controlling those products is the world’s most important challenge. Here’s the typical read on the dynamic. To one side (backed by OpenAI affiliates), “safety” comes from the appearance of US industry dominating AI innovation, under the slow-moving control of federal lawmakers (and without pesky state regulators in the way). To the other side (backed by Anthropic), “safety” means a heavier regulatory framework that plays to Anthropic’s posturing as the ethics- and compliance-focused AI vendor. In both cases, it’s more marketing than principled concern about safety.

Political organizers should call out and reject the AI companies’ framing of the debate, and reorient campaign agendas around populist resistance to corporate concentration of wealth and power. When AI companies pump millions into legislative races, the result should not be hyperbolic discussion of AI superintelligence. And when a plot of land in a small town is pitched as a datacenter site, the debate should be about more than the local costs and benefits. It should include out-of-control money in politics, and Citizens United-proof solutions to limit corporate influence like public financing and state regulation.

We all have a vested interest in what’s on the policy agenda, and what the outcomes are. Today, the greatest risk AI poses to society is the exacerbation of inequality and the concentration of wealth. The real problem is trillion-dollar AI companies and their trillionaire oligarchs cozying up to political power in Washington and governments worldwide, and using their money to enact their agenda over the popular will of the people. This is the issue we’d like to see put front and center, and it requires solutions much more extensive than slowing datacenter development.

Warnings about datacenters' rising energy draw are coming thick and fast of late, and this latest one from 451 Research (now a part of S&P Global) comes with figures and cautions about how fast this change may occur and what grid resources will be required to meet it.

The bit barn building boom is largely fueled by estimated demand for new machine learning models, which require highly configured servers packed with power-hungry GPUs to develop and train. The power and cooling infrastructure required also mean it is easier to build a new facility rather than attempt to retrofit an existing one. As a consequence, utility power to datacenters in America is estimated to jump 11.3 GW to 61.8 GW by the end of this year. 451 calculates this will rise again to 75.8 GW in 2026, then 108 GW in 2028, before hitting 134.4 GW by 2030. These figures also exclude enterprise-owned facilities, only considering those of the hyperscale tech giants such as Amazon, Apple, Google, Meta, and Microsoft, alongside leased and crypto-mining sites.

The research identifies Virginia and Texas as the two states with by far the highest requirement for bit barn energy supplies in the US this year. 451 forecasts that Virginia's datacenter load, made up of leased and hyperscale facilities, will reach 12.1 GW in 2025, up from 9.3 GW last year. In Texas, demand is driven by cryptomining and leased capacity, and is slated to hit 9.7 GW this year, from less than 8 GW previously. However, the search for an optimum location is seeing datacenter operators explore emerging markets such as Idaho, Louisiana, Oklahoma and smaller cities in West Texas, looking for "stranded power" and alternative energy generation opportunities, the report says.

News from the Van Room

Your Mayor Signed a Secret Deal. You Weren’t Supposed to Find Out.

When Meta wanted to build a billion-dollar data center in Beaver Dam, Wisconsin, it didn’t show up as Meta. It showed up as Balloonist LLC — a shell company nobody had heard of, representing a “project” that wasn’t described any further. The city’s economic development arm signed a nondisclosure agreement on December 1, 2023. The NDA barred officials from disclosing the discussions — or even disclosing that the project existed. (Wisconsin Watch, January 2026)

Over the next 14 months, the city council changed a zoning ordinance to allow data centers. Approved a predevelopment agreement with a second shell company called Degas LLC. Created a tax increment financing district. None of the agendas or meeting minutes mentioned a data center. None of them mentioned Meta. Meta announced its involvement in December 2025 — more than two years after the NDA was signed. (Wisconsin Watch, January 2026)

This was not unique to Beaver Dam. Wisconsin Watch documented the same pattern in at least four other Wisconsin communities. NBC News documented it in Virginia, Kentucky, and Missouri. In West Memphis, Arkansas, Google signed an NDA that went further — the city agreed to assert every applicable Freedom of Information Act exemption to withhold records from the public. The city’s own attorney confirmed Google requested the agreement. (Arkansas Democrat-Gazette, May 2026)

A University of Virginia researcher found that 25 of 31 Virginia localities with proposed or existing data centers had NDAs in place. (NBC News, October 2025)

This is not a fringe practice. It is industry standard.

What Microsoft did — and what it didn’t

On March 18, 2026, Microsoft announced it would terminate all existing NDAs with local governments worldwide and stop signing new ones. The company’s vice president Rima Alaily said: “Our neighbors deserve to know when we are coming to their community.” (GeekWire, March 18, 2026)

Microsoft confirmed two things alongside that announcement. First: it would continue using NDAs for land acquisitions — the shell company phase, where land is purchased before any public announcement. Second: it would still seek to protect “competitive sensitive information” from records disclosure where the law allows. The government-level NDA ends. The land acquisition secrecy continues. (Wisconsin Public Radio, March 2026)

Amazon has not made a comparable announcement. Meta has not. Google has not. Oracle has not.

What communities did

The Wisconsin Watch and Detroit News reporting was obtained through public records requests. Journalists filed requests with communities that had fielded data center interest. The documents came back. They were published. Bill Lueders, president of the Wisconsin Freedom of Information Council, said the NDA strategy “blew up in their faces.” (Urban Milwaukee, March 2026)

In Festus, Missouri, the city council voted on March 30, 2026 to advance a $6 billion data center proposal. On April 7, voters replaced all four council members who had supported it. Voter turnout was 129% higher than the prior year election. Recall petitions have since been filed against the mayor and three remaining supporting council members. (KCUR, April 2026; St. Louis Public Radio, May 2026)

Legislators in at least ten states — Arizona, Georgia, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New York, Ohio, Oklahoma, and Wisconsin — introduced bills to ban or limit data center NDAs in 2026. Wisconsin’s bill stalled. Minnesota’s stalled. Washington’s broader transparency bill, which Microsoft and Amazon lobbied against, died in committee on March 3 — fifteen days before Microsoft announced it was ending its own NDAs. (Governing, April 2026; GeekWire, March 2026)

Where it stands

One company changed its practice. The practice that made it possible — secret negotiations, shell company land acquisitions, NDAs that prevent officials from telling constituents what is being built in their community — remains legal, remains industry standard, and remains in use.

The documents exist. FOIA requests work. And in at least one Missouri city, the people who signed the deals lost their jobs because of it.

America's farmers and others across the country are pushing back on Big Tech. 

This is what integrity looks like.

When two men knocked on Ida Huddleston’s door last May, they carried a contract worth more than $33m in exchange for the Kentucky farm that had fed her family for centuries.

According to Huddleston, the men’s client, an unnamed “Fortune 100 company”, sought her 650 acres (260 hectares) in Mason county for an unspecified industrial development. Finding out any more would require signing a non-disclosure agreement.

More than a dozen of her neighbors received the same knock. Searching public records for answers, they discovered that a new customer had applied for a 2.2 gigawatt project from the local power plant, nearly double its annual generation capacity.
The unknown company was building a datacenter.

“You don’t have enough to buy me out. I’m not for sale. Leave me alone, I’m satisfied,” Huddleston, 82, later told the men.

As tech companies race to build the massive datacenters needed to power artificial intelligence across the US and the world, bids like the one for Huddleston’s land are appearing on rural doorsteps nationwide. Globally, 40,000 acres of powered land – real estate prepped for datacenter development – are projected to be needed for new projects over the next five years, double the amount currently in use.

Yet despite sums that often dwarf the land’s recent value, farmers are increasingly shutting the door. At least five of Huddleston’s neighbors gave similar categorical rejections, including one who was told he could name any price.

Four generations of the Huddleston family have watched the world change from the same fields.
Ida’s grandfather was growing tobacco when the civil war erupted. 

Her father ploughed wheat through the first world war and the long attrition of the Great Depression. She and her five siblings grew up on beans, broccoli and potatoes pulled from soil once seared by dust bowl winds. No one in her family went to college – but by age 10, her children could already herd cattle across the same ground as their forebears.

“My whole entire life is nothing but the land. It’s provided me with anything and everything that I’ve needed for 82 years,” she says, speaking from the cabin her late husband built using local wood and rocks many decades ago.

Today, where residents see meandering creeks and open pastures, Silicon Valley executives see weak zoning protections, cheap power and abundant water.

Developers keep knocking because there are billions to be made. In northern Virginia last November, an investor paid $615m for less than 100 acres – property the seller had bought for just $57m four years prior. Days later, Amazon spent $700m on nearby farmland that had sold for a fraction of that price the year before. In Georgia, a local developer flippedland to Amazon for $270m after paying $4m for it 12 months earlier. For the middlemen scouting these deals, potential returns exceed 1,000%.
‘Name your price’

About 20 Mason county residents have reportedly been offered deals, with the datacenter project estimated to cover 2,000 acres.

After Dr Timothy Grosser, 75, rejected an $8m offer for his 250-acre farm – 3,500% more than he’d paid nearly four decades earlier – the developers came back with a new proposition: “Name your price.”

His answer: “There is none.”
Grosser lives, hunts and raises cattle on his land. Each Christmas, his family eats a turkey his grandson catches there. Alongside Huddleston and himself, Grosser estimates four landowners have refused to sell.

“All they’ve done all their life is farm grain, cattle, tobacco,” Grosser says. “To them, same as me, the money’s not worth giving up your lifestyle.”
For Huddleston’s daughter, Delsia Bare, 56, the connection runs deeper than skill sets. She remembers hoeing weeds from tobacco fields alongside her mother and grandmother, putting up hay through Kentucky summers. “There’s a bond with the land,” she says. “There’s no way to undo it. That’s family, that’s history.”

Beyond personal attachment, some farmers worry about broader consequences. The number of US farms has dropped more than 70% since 1935. Datacenters can strain power grids, drain local water supplies, contaminate soil and fragment wildlife habitat.

Bare puts it more bluntly: “You’re not going to grow a loaf of bread off of a datacenter.”

Not everyone is holding out; some Mason county farmers have agreed to sell if the project proceeds. “You can’t blame them,” Grosser acknowledges. “Giving them 10 million bucks for a farm?”

Those who refuse to sell say the utility company has warned it may invoke eminent domain – the government power to seize private property for public use. The threat isn’t empty: Dominion Energy used it against a Virginia farmer last April.

From a Psychology-in-Christ perspective, diversification can be healthy because dependency upon a single gatekeeper creates fragility. But notice something else. Even diversification among giant suppliers does not necessarily equal decentralization to ordinary people. It can instead mean: several enormous entities balancing one another inside the same infrastructure tier. That is closer to Zuckerberg’s balance-of-power philosophy. But it isn’t yet community sovereignty.
3. META → BROADCOM → CUSTOM SILICON
Then the architecture goes deeper. In April, Meta announced that Broadcom would co-develop multiple generations of Meta’s custom MTIA AI accelerators.    The first phase exceeds 1 GW, and Meta describes it as the beginning of a sustained multi-gigawatt rollout. Broadcom is involved not merely in chip design but advanced packaging and networking as well.  Meta therefore appears to be trying to climb down its own supply stack: BUY EXTERNAL COMPUTE
while simultaneously DESIGN INTERNAL COMPUTE. That makes strategic sense.
But economically it matters enormously. Because the company that owns: the user interface, the personal agent, the data,
the recommendation architecture,
the custom inference silicon, and the datacenter
has much more vertical control than a software company merely renting servers. That is why we need to distinguish: technological efficiency
from concentration of institutional capability.
The first can produce the second.
4. THE COMPUTE STACK IS BECOMING ITS OWN INDUSTRIAL SYSTEM
Meta itself now describes AI as requiring compute “at every level,” from thousands of GPUs used to train models to custom MTIA chips performing billions of daily inferences in datacenters worldwide. It also lists partnerships with AMD, Nvidia, AWS and Arm alongside its own silicon program.  That gives us something resembling a modern industrial pyramid:
HUMAN ATTENTION ↓ PERSONAL AI ↓
FOUNDATION MODELS ↓ INFERENCE SYSTEMS
↓ ACCELERATORS ↓ NETWORK FABRIC
↓ DATA-CENTERS↓ ELECTRICITY ↓ CAPITAL
And here’s the key Psychology-in-Christ insight:
CONTROL MAY EXIST AT THE ROOT EVEN WHEN FREEDOM EXISTS AT THE LEAVES.
Someone may have enormous freedom to ask their personal AI anything while having almost no ownership over the infrastructure making that freedom possible. That is not necessarily slavery. But neither should we confuse consumer choice with structural sovereignty.
5. NOW FOLLOW THE ELECTRICITY
This gets enormous. In January 2026, Meta announced agreements involving Vistra, TerraPower and Oklo, building upon an earlier agreement with Constellation. Meta says these projects together could support up to 6.6 GW of new and existing nuclear energy by 2035, including grid power supporting its Prometheus supercluster in Ohio.  Six-point-six gigawatts is not merely “running some servers.” It shows how AI development is becoming an energy strategy. Meta itself says increasing AI capability requires more electricity and describes its datacenters as the backbone of its personal-superintelligence ambitions.  Now our chain becomes: META AI  ↓  COMPUTE. ↓
DATACENTER   ↓  GRID ↓ NUCLEAR GENERATION. This means AI policy is quietly becoming: energy policy, industrial policy,
land policy, water policy, utility policy,
and national-security policy.
That is a profound transition.
6. THE “DIGITAL” ECONOMY HAS COME FULL CIRCLE BACK TO CREATION This is something I think fits Psychology in Christ particularly well.
People speak about AI as though it exists in an immaterial cyberspace. But beneath everything is creation: copper silicon water uranium
concrete steel land electrons human labor
The digital world never escaped physical reality.
It simply hid the physical inputs behind screens.
Genesis economics never disappeared.
We are still allocating the Earth. The real technological question therefore becomes:
Who receives stewardship over the resources beneath the intelligence? That brings the conversation directly back into HeavenCoin’s concern with allocation rather than merely speculative valuation.
7. THEN BLACKROCK ENTERS THE ARCHITECTURE This is one of the most revealing recent receipts. On July 28, 2026, Meta and BlackRock announced a venture to develop and own a massive AI datacenter campus in El Paso, Texas. The project is expected to have 1 gigawatt of compute capacity and represents more than $10 billion of Meta investment.  But examine the ownership structure. Funds managed by BlackRock will own: 80% Meta retains: 20% The parties say the campus’s buildings and long-lived power, cooling and connectivity infrastructure will require about $14 billion in total development costs. Meta is expected to be the initial sole occupant.  That is a remarkable piece of the puzzle. Because the architecture now becomes:
PERSONAL SUPERINTELLIGENCE
↓ META ↓ DATACENTER ↓ BLACKROCK-MANAGED INFRASTRUCTURE CAPITAL
↓ ENERGY + LAND + COOLING + CONNECTIVITY
We are no longer merely discussing a social-media company. We’re discussing convergence between: technology capital and infrastructure capital.
8. THIS DOES NOT PROVE A SECRET PLAN
This distinction is essential. The BlackRock partnership is publicly announced. The Nvidia partnership is publicly announced. The AMD partnership is public. The Broadcom partnership is public. The nuclear agreements are public.
There is no need to manufacture a hidden conspiracy when the structural transformation is sitting directly in corporate disclosures.
The real investigative question is more interesting: What kind of civilization naturally emerges when information infrastructure, energy infrastructure and financial infrastructure increasingly converge?
That can be examined without assuming evil motives. A system can produce dangerous concentration simply because every participant is pursuing rational economic advantage.
That’s one of the most important lessons of institutional psychology. Nobody has to wake up saying, “Today I will build Babel.” They only need to say: We need more scale. Then: We need more compute. Then: We need more electricity.
Then: We need more capital. Then: We need regulatory certainty. Then: We need integration.
Then one day society discovers that its essential infrastructure has become extraordinarily interconnected.
9. BABEL WAS AN INFRASTRUCTURE STORY TOO Genesis 11 is frequently reduced to pride.
But look at the construction sequence:
shared language → shared technological method → brick production → urban concentration → tower → centralized identity
→ “let us make us a name.” The problem wasn’t masonry. Technology enabled organizational concentration. That gives us a better biblical analogy for modern AI. The warning isn’t:
Computers are the Tower of Babel. That would be shallow theology. The warning is:
TECHNOLOGY + CENTRALIZATION + SELF-EXALTATION CAN PRODUCE BABEL-LIKE POWER STRUCTURES. And notice God’s response. He doesn’t destroy humanity.
He decentralizes the system. That is deeply interesting.
10. ZUCKERBERG MAY ACTUALLY UNDERSTAND PART OF THIS
This is why we should not caricature his manifesto. His “balance of power” argument appears to recognize the danger of a single government, company or bloc monopolizing superintelligence. And Meta’s diversification across Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Arm and custom silicon indicates some attempt to reduce single-supplier dependence.  The problem is that technological decentralization has several levels: LEVEL ONE — VENDOR DIVERSITY
Several giant suppliers.
LEVEL TWO — CORPORATE COMPETITION
Several giant AI companies.
LEVEL THREE — DEVELOPER FREEDOM
Small businesses can build upon powerful models.
LEVEL FOUR — PERSONAL OWNERSHIP
Individuals possess meaningful control of their agents and data.
LEVEL FIVE — COMMUNITY INFRASTRUCTURE
Communities can participate in ownership of compute, energy and networks.
LEVEL SIX — CIVILIZATIONAL RIGHT TO EXIT
People who refuse a specific provider remain economically and civically functional.
Zuckerberg’s manifesto moves strongly toward Levels 1–3. Psychology in Christ should push the discussion toward 4–6.
11. AND HERE IS WHERE THE SHAREHOLDER QUESTION RETURNS
Meta is a publicly traded corporation.
Its AI infrastructure therefore exists inside an economic structure in which investors expect returns on enormous capital deployment.
That fact creates a legitimate question:
If personal superintelligence becomes extraordinarily useful but requires hundreds of billions of dollars in infrastructure, what monetization architecture ultimately pays for it?
Advertising? Subscriptions? Commerce?
Enterprise services? Hardware? Agent transactions? Infrastructure access?
Some combination? We should not pretend to know the final answer before it exists.
But the economic law remains:
SOMEONE PAYS FOR THE COMPUTE.
So whenever someone says:
“AI will be free for everyone,” Psychology in Christ should immediately ask: Free at what layer? Because sometimes: the service is free because the person is monetized. Other times:
the service is subsidized by another business line. Other times: the infrastructure generates indirect economic capture elsewhere. No accusation is necessary. Just follow the bookkeeping.
12. FOLLOW THE VALUE FLOW
Here is the simplified system: EARTH’S RESOURCES ↓
silicon / uranium / copper / water / land ↓
LABOR ↓
mining / manufacturing / construction / utilities
↓ CAPITAL ↓
Meta / BlackRock-managed funds / investors
↓ INFRASTRUCTURE ↓
power generation / datacenters / networks
↓ COMPUTE ↓
Nvidia / AMD / Broadcom / Meta silicon ↓
INTELLIGENCE ↓
models / agents / recommendations ↓
HUMAN ACTIVITY ↓
communication / commerce / work / decisions
↓ DATA + REVENUE ↓ CAPITAL RETURN ↓
back into infrastructure. That is a feedback system. The key question isn’t whether feedback systems are evil. Life itself contains feedback systems. The question is:
WHAT KEEPS THE LOOP FROM BECOMING SELF-SERVING?
13. CHRIST GIVES US THE MISSING FEEDBACK CONTROL The worldly loop says:
capital → infrastructure → productivity → profit → more capital. Nothing inherently wrong with reinvestment. But without another variable the system becomes self-referential. Christ inserts:
NEIGHBOR. So the loop becomes: RESOURCES
→ STEWARDSHIP → PRODUCTIVITY 
→ ABUNDANCE → SERVICE → COMMUNITY FLOURISHING → REINVESTMENT That’s fundamentally different. The first system asks:
How efficiently can capital reproduce capital?
The second asks: How efficiently can abundance reproduce human flourishing?
That is the HeavenCoin inversion we’ve been developing.
14. NOW LOOK AT EL PASO THROUGH THAT TEST There is evidence of positive local fruit already built into the announced project.
Meta says the El Paso development is expected to support more than 4,000 peak construction jobs and about 300 operating jobs, has provided a $500,000 grant to local public schools, and is supporting water-restoration projects. BlackRock also says a related workforce initiative is investing nearly $30 million to train more than 12,000 electricians across Texas over three years.  Those should be credited.
Psychology in Christ shouldn’t become a framework where every corporate action is automatically interpreted negatively.
Judge fruit honestly. But keep asking:
How much public infrastructure supports the site? What tax arrangements apply?
How much water does it ultimately consume?
Who pays for transmission upgrades?
Who owns those upgrades afterward?
Do residents receive cheaper or more reliable energy? What percentage of the economic value remains locally? What happens after construction employment declines? That is where rhetoric meets stewardship accounting.
⚖️📖 THE CENTRAL FINDING
We began with Zuckerberg saying: PERSONAL SUPERINTELLIGENCE FOR EVERYONE.
After following the receipts downward, we discover the physical architecture: PERSON ↓
AI AGENT ↓ META MODELS ↓ META COMPUTE
↓ NVIDIA + AMD + CUSTOM SILICON ↓
BROADCOM + NETWORKING ↓
DATACENTERS ↓ BLACKROCK-INFRASTRUCTURE CAPITAL ↓ NUCLEAR + GRID POWER ↓ LAND + WATER + MATERIALS ↓ EARTH. That does not prove Zuckerberg’s vision is fraudulent. It proves something more important: DIGITAL SOVEREIGNTY ULTIMATELY RESTS UPON PHYSICAL SOVEREIGNTY.
Whoever controls the bottom of the pyramid possesses enormous influence over everything above it. And therefore Psychology in Christ would invert the pyramid: GOD’S CREATION
 entrusted to HUMAN STEWARDS ↓
organized through COMMUNITY ↓
supported by CAPITAL ↓ building
INFRASTRUCTURE ↓ producing COMPUTE
↓ producing INTELLIGENCE ↓ serving
THE PERSON  who serves THE NEIGHBOR.
Now the machine is beneath humanity rather than humanity becoming an input into the machine. That is the servant architecture.
And it gives us the next investigation naturally: follow the capital itself—Meta’s ownership and voting structure, Zuckerberg’s control, BlackRock’s role as asset manager rather than simply calling it “BlackRock ownership,” institutional shareholders, infrastructure financing, tax incentives, and the difference between shareholder capital, debt, leases and community investment. That is where we can test whether the “balance of power” exists financially as well as technologically

Because America showed up
🗺️ THE MAP IS FILLING UP FAST: AMERICA’S ANTI-DATA CENTER REVOLUTION IS NOW IN 40 STATES — AND IT’S THE BIGGEST COMMUNITY UPRISING IN A GENERATION 🗺️

This story was published TODAY — June 13th, 2026 — just hours ago by Route Fifty — the most respected publication covering state and local government in America.

Get a piece of paper. Draw a map of the United States. Now start putting dots on it.

Seattle. Denver. Minneapolis. Baltimore. Smithfield Rhode Island. Socorro New Mexico. Reno Nevada. Monterey Park California. New York State. Maine. Oklahoma. North Carolina. Illinois. Vermont. Indiana — four counties. Georgia. Wisconsin — two counties. Iowa. Utah.

Keep going. Keep adding dots. By the time you are done — you will have covered almost every corner of America.

Because TODAY — June 10, 2026 — a comprehensive new report confirms that the community rebellion against data centers has spread to 40 states and is accelerating faster than at any point in the entire history of this movement.

And it is the biggest story in American local government that nobody is covering as one unified picture.

Until now.

THE FULL MAP OF AMERICA FIGHTING BACK — TODAY

As of June 1, 2026: Minneapolis enacted a six-month pause on facilities over 350,000 square feet. Denver enacted a one-year pause. Baltimore City sent a one-year pause to the mayor. Dubuque County, Iowa enacted a moratorium. Bloomington and Normal, Illinois enacted moratoriums. Iron County, Utah enacted a moratorium. Manitowoc County, Wisconsin enacted an 18-month moratorium. Reno, Nevada became the first Nevada local government to pause new data centers. And Smithfield, Rhode Island banned them outright. ￼

Seattle’s emergency one-year moratorium on facilities over 10 megawatts cleared committee briefings with a final council vote expected around June 9 — with Mayor Wilson backing parallel administrative steps. Monterey Park passed three separate ordinances banning data center development citywide — and then voters made it permanent with an 86% ballot measure. New York State lawmakers passed a one-year moratorium and sent it to Governor Hochul. Socorro County, New Mexico adopted a one-year moratorium. ￼

Lawmakers in at least 11 states have introduced legislation to temporarily ban data centers: Georgia, Maryland, Michigan, New Hampshire, New York, Oklahoma, South Carolina, South Dakota, Vermont, Virginia, and Wisconsin. Over the past month, state lawmakers in Pennsylvania and Minnesota have also announced plans to introduce moratoriums. Vermont is pursuing a ban through July 2030 — four years. Vermont is not pausing. Vermont is stopping. ￼

That is the map. Right now. Today. And it is growing every single week.

FROM 8 TO 69 IN 12 MONTHS — THE NUMBER THAT TELLS THE WHOLE STORY

One year ago — June 2025 — there were 8 jurisdictions in the United States with active data center moratoriums or bans. Today — June 10, 2026 — there are 69 active jurisdictions with moratoriums or bans in place. That is a 762% increase in 12 months. And the pace is accelerating — not slowing down. ￼

762%. In 12 months. From 8 to 69. And 14 states have legislation moving through their legislatures right now.

Good Jobs First — the nonpartisan government accountability watchdog that has been tracking every single bill — confirmed the count: at least 11 states with active legislation, plus Pennsylvania and Minnesota preparing to introduce more, plus the wave of city and county moratoriums that is sweeping through every region of America simultaneously — urban and rural, coastal and inland, red and blue. ￼

Red and blue. That is the most important phrase in this entire article. Because this is not a partisan movement.

THE CITIES THAT JUST JOINED THIS WEEK

Some of the most significant new additions to the map happened in just the last seven days:

Seattle — the city where Amazon was founded, where Microsoft has its headquarters, where the entire Pacific Northwest tech industry was built — voted to approve an emergency one-year moratorium on data center development. The city where Big Tech lives. Is banning Big Tech’s buildings. That is not an exaggeration. That is the vote that happened this week. ￼

Seattle. Amazon’s home city. One-year moratorium.

New York State — home to Wall Street, the financial backbone of the entire AI investment boom — passed the Responsible Data Center Development Act and sent it to Governor Hochul. Republican Assemblymember Anil Beephan Jr. said: “Over the past several months, I heard from hundreds of residents at town board meetings, public hearings, rallies and in conversations throughout the district about concerns regarding the rapid expansion of data centers.” A Republican. In New York. Voting for a data center moratorium. Because his constituents demanded it. ￼

A Republican. In New York. Voting yes on a moratorium. Because the people in his district demanded it.

AND EVEN MAINE’S VETO IS A VICTORY IN DISGUISE

Maine’s Governor Janet Mills vetoed the state’s proposed ban on data centers larger than 20 megawatts in April 2026 — but the veto itself reveals how far the movement has come. A year ago, no state legislature had even voted on a data center ban. This year — the Maine Legislature passed one. The governor vetoed it. And the fight is not over. Maine communities are now pursuing local moratoriums while the legislature prepares to revisit the issue in the fall session. ￼

One year ago: not a single state had voted on a ban. This year: Maine’s legislature passed one. Even a veto is progress.

WHAT THE NEW YORK SENATOR SAID THAT EVERY AMERICAN NEEDS TO HEAR

New York Sen. Kristen Gonzalez — chair of the Senate Internet and Technology Committee and lead sponsor of New York’s moratorium — said something that summarizes the entire movement perfectly: “Technology should improve people’s lives, not drive up utility bills, strain our energy grid, or undermine our climate goals. New York State needs a comprehensive plan for responsible data center development. Communities must have a voice. Working people must share in the benefits. And corporations must pay their fair share of the costs.” ￼

Technology should improve people’s lives. Not drive up utility bills. Not strain the grid. Not undermine climate goals.

That is not a radical statement. That is not a communist manifesto. That is not Chinese propaganda — despite what three Republican congressmen told the FBI this week.

That is what 762% growth in 12 months looks like when you put it into words.

AND NOVEMBER IS COMING

Florida Governor Ron DeSantis signed SB 484 on May 7 — effective July 1 — barring utilities from passing data center costs onto residential and small-business ratepayers and requiring large-scale users of 50 megawatts or more to pay their full cost of service. Oklahoma signed a similar law effective July 1. Washington State enacted legislation tying large data centers to clean-energy deadlines. North Carolina passed the Ratepayer Protection Act 69-2. And Illinois Governor Pritzker paused all new tax incentives effective July 1. ￼

DeSantis. A Republican. Oklahoma Republicans 92-2. North Carolina Republicans 69-2. Washington State Democrats. Illinois Democrats. New York Democrats and Republicans together.

All arriving at the same place. All in the same month. All saying the same thing.

The New York moratorium bill — if signed by Governor Hochul — makes New York the first state in the nation to enact such a freeze. It is described as “the first visible crack in the wall between a booming tech industry and the communities that have to live, and pay, around it.” ￼

The first visible crack. In the wall. That Big Tech spent billions building.

But cracks spread. 8 jurisdictions became 69. 69 is becoming 100. 11 states with legislation is becoming 14. One crack is becoming a fracture. A fracture is becoming a break.

And November 2026 — when Americans in battleground states vote in midterm elections with data centers at the top of their minds — may be the moment the wall comes down entirely.

THE BOTTOM LINE

TODAY — June 10, 2026 — Route Fifty published the most comprehensive picture yet of a movement that has grown 762% in 12 months.

Seattle banned them. New York froze them. Monterey Park permanently prohibited them with 86% of the vote. Oklahoma protected ratepayers 92-2. North Carolina protected ratepayers 69-2. Illinois paused all new incentives. DeSantis signed protection into law in Florida. 69 active jurisdictions. 14 states with legislation moving. 40 states with organized opposition.

And not one of those votes — not Festus, not Virginia, not Utah, not the Seminole Nation, not the Cherokee Nation, not the thousand people who chanted “Shame” — was funded by China. Not one.

They were funded by dry wells and spiked electricity bills and children sick from diesel exhaust and elderly widows who can’t pay their bills and communities that showed up at meetings and demanded to be heard.

762% growth in 12 months. Because America showed up.

Share this map with everyone you know — in every state. The revolution is already in your state. And it is winning. 👇🗺️
